title: Design System: One Tool to Rule Them All — Quarto Workshop
text:
The site and the ZALF deck share the look of the ZALF Science Conference 2026 website (science-conference.zalf.de): a mint ground, forest-green headings and dark bands, slanted section edges and rounded white surfaces. The type is the DML brand pair (iat-dml/dml-brand-yml): DM Serif Display for headings, DM Sans for text. The DML mark sits in the navbar and the slide corner, the full DML lockup in the footer.
The site is itself a showcase of Quarto output, so it must look like something a careful researcher would publish. On the homepage the design carries the message; on interior reference pages findability comes first and the colour is held back.
Chosen in November 2026 from three mock-ups (institutional ZALF frame, conference look, editorial ZALF gradient). The institutional design system in iat-zalf-slides was judged too plain for a workshop site; this system keeps its greens and its restraint but takes the conference’s typography and shapes.
Key characteristics

White pages, with mint for homepage bands, slide grounds, callouts and the closed exercise steps.
Forest (#153D31) for headings and dark bands; green (#2F7F43) for links and buttons; leaf (#4A9E48) only for bullets, underlines and large shapes.
Two typefaces and a mono: serif to display, sans to read, mono for code.
Slanted edges on full-width bands, never on cards.
One light theme. There is no dark mode.




All colours live in _brand.yml. styles.scss and revealjs.scss expose each one as a CSS variable named after its brand token (--ds-mint, --ds-forest, …); use those, never hex values, in rules and markup.








Token
Hex
Use




mint
#EFF8E5
Homepage bands, slide ground, callouts, closed exercise steps, the active sidebar item


mint-deep
#DDEFCB
Open exercise step header and its border, inline code


mint-pale
#F5F8F2
Code blocks, sidebar hover


leaf
#4A9E48
Bullet markers, active TOC rule, large shapes. Not for text: 3.4:1 on white


green
#2F7F43
Links, primary buttons, italic emphasis in titles, labels on cards (4.9:1 on white)


forest
#153D31
Headings, outline buttons, dark bands (with forest-2 as a 135° gradient), footer


ink
#16322B
Body text


muted
#53675E
Secondary text, captions (6.1:1 on white, 5.5:1 on mint)


sage-light, leaf-light
#CFE3C8, #A9DB8F
Secondary text and links on forest


teal-ink, amber, red

Strings in code, warning text, important and caution text



The tint marks what you can open or what stands apart. Long reading happens on white. Mint fills callouts and the closed exercise steps; on the homepage it alternates with white and forest bands. A mint surface never sits on a mint band: on mint, surfaces are white.




DM Serif Display (one weight, 400, with italic): page titles, h1 to h4, card titles, team names, exercise step titles, slide titles. Its weight is fixed, so hierarchy comes from size alone.
DM Sans (400 to 700): body text, navigation, buttons, h5 and h6, callout headers, sidebar and TOC labels.
IBM Plex Mono: code.

Italic in a title (*Rule Them All*) renders in green. Labels are sentence case in DM Sans 600; nothing is set in capitals, and there are no eyebrow labels above headings.




Slanted edges (--ds-cut, up to 72px): full-width homepage bands, the footer, the title slide’s band and the dividers’ mint wedge. Each band overlaps the previous one by one cut.
Radii: 18px for cards and the video frame, 12px for callouts and code, 14px for exercise steps, pills for buttons.
Shadow: one soft forest shadow (--ds-shadow) under white surfaces on mint, and a deeper one on hover for clickable cards, which also rise by 3px. Shadows are mixed from forest, never black.
Borders: hairlines only, mixed from forest. No coloured side stripes.






White navbar with a hairline shadow, the DML mark (assets/dml-mark.svg) and “Quarto workshop” in the serif. No active underline: with one sidebar for the whole site, Quarto marks the first item active on every page. The footer is a forest band with a slanted top, the DML lockup for dark grounds (assets/dml-lockup-dark.png, rendered from dml-strata-lockup-deep-dark.svg with its fonts baked in) and two links.



Built from full-width divs in index.qmd: .home-band with --white, --mint or --forest, the hero .home-hero, and .home-band--last before the footer. Inside, .home-wrap holds the 70rem content width. The hero has the title, subtitle, three buttons and .home-video, a 16:9 frame with a white border that holds a placeholder until the shortened pitch video replaces it (instructions in the comment above it). The event box is white because the conference logo has a white ground.



White cards on the mint band: serif title as a stretched link, description in muted, a green line (“Guide and exercise”) at the foot. No icons.



{.step} headings become <details> panels (assets/step-accordion.html). Closed steps are mint bars with the step title in the serif; the open step has a mint-deep header over a white body with a mint-deep border. The “Open all steps” button is a forest outline pill.



Mint fill, no frame, header in DM Sans 600 coloured by type: forest (note), green (tip), amber (warning), red (important, caution). On slides they are white.



Inline: mint-deep fill, forest-2 text. Blocks: mint-pale with a hairline on the site, white panels with a shadow on slides. Syntax colours come from the palette (keywords forest, functions green, strings teal-ink, comments muted italic, numbers amber).



Mint ground; content panels, code, callouts and the .rendered output are white. Slide titles in the serif, forest. The DML mark sits bottom right via logo: in the deck’s YAML; Quarto then moves the slide number to the top right. Footer and mark are hidden on the title slide and on dividers.

Title slide (title-style: editorial): event logo top left (event: logo:), the title with its italic part on its own line in green, the subtitle in DM Sans, and a forest band across the foot with the presenter and event.tagline. The band is drawn inside the slide and runs past its edges, so the text stays on it at any aspect ratio.
Dividers (# Title {.divider}): forest gradient with a mint wedge rising to the right. The deck’s background-color attributes are overridden from the stylesheet, so they need no editing.
Checkpoints: the current step has a green numbered disc, earlier steps a mint-deep tick.
Agenda (.agenda > .agenda-row): time in green, the part in the serif over a muted line, a green bar on a white timeline track and the length. Each row sets --start and --len in minutes.
Question (.question): a question to the room, large and vertically centred, with prompts underneath.
Tabsets: tabs as DM Sans 600 text with a green rule under the open tab; the content on a white panel.
Screen recordings (img.screencast): GIFs in assets/screencasts/, made by _screencasts/record-screencasts.py from the rendered site. Re-record them when the home page or the deck changes visibly.
Lists in the ZALF deck have 0.6em between items (slides/zalf-2026.scss), except the checkpoint steps and the mock output in .rendered.





Do - Take every colour and font from _brand.yml through the --ds-* variables. - Keep interior pages white; use mint for callouts, steps and homepage bands. - Put white surfaces on mint and mint surfaces on white. - Check text against WCAG 2.1 AA: leaf and mint-deep are never text colours on white. - Give every transition a prefers-reduced-motion fallback and keep visible focus rings.
Don’t - Bring back the old Quartile Press system (warm paper, Newsreader, IBM Plex Sans, indigo/coral/moss/amber). - Add a third typeface, set headings in capitals or put eyebrow labels above headings. - Use coloured side stripes, gradient text, glassmorphism or decorative icons. - Slant cards or panels; slants belong to full-width bands only. - Add a dark theme without drawing and contrast-checking a full dark palette first.

title: One Tool to Rule Them All
text:
Why ?

Research produces many related outputs: Notes, manuscripts, slides etc.
These are usually made with disconnected tools and manual formatting
Quarto lets you write once in plain text, render to HTML, PDF, DOCX, slides, and more
Focus on content, not juggling tools

title: One Tool to Rule Them All
text:
Workshop Structure

Foundations — Quarto, Markdown, YAML
Academic use cases:




Research Diary
Documenting your research in a reproducible way from the very beginning.



Manuscripts
Write in plain text; render to PDF, HTML, or DOCX, then share with collaborators.



Presentations
Build reveal.js talks from the same source as your research.



Websites
Project, lab, and personal websites to improve outreach.



Dashboards
Interactive dashboards for exploring and communicating your research.



Each use case has a guided exercise which you will have time to test today.


Advanced Topics: Templates, multi-lingual outputs, consistent branding, AI assistance and more

title: One Tool to Rule Them All
text:
What Is ?

Open-source scientific publishing system from Posit
The multi-language, multi-format successor to R Markdown
Three ingredients in one .qmd file:

YAML for metadata and configuration
Markdown for written content
Code chunks (R, Python, Julia, OJS) for computation

title: One Tool to Rule Them All
text:
Key Benefits

Plain text: every change is a visible, trackable line (version control friendly)
One source, many outputs: HTML, PDF, DOCX, slides from the same file
Executable code: results are computed at render time, not pasted in
Familiar if you know LaTeX, but simpler markup and more output formats

title: One Tool to Rule Them All
text:
Markdown in 30 Seconds

Lightweight syntax for structure: headings, lists, links, images, emphasis
# Title, ## Section, **bold**, *italic*, [link](url)
Quarto adds academic extras: citations, cross-references, callouts, figures with captions
Mindset: describe what things are, let the renderer handle how they look

title: One Tool to Rule Them All
text:
YAML: Configuring Your Document

The block between --- fences at the top of a file
Controls title, authors, date, output format, and options

---
title: "My Analysis"
author: "Jane Doe"
format: pdf
---

Key : value pairs; indentation matters
Same content, different YAML = different publication

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
Approximate speaking time: 6–6½ minutes at a calm pace.


Keep returning to this one mental model:

A Quarto source combines Markdown for the content, YAML for the configuration, and, when useful, code for computed results. Quarto renders that source into the output you need.

The deliberately modest version of the promise is one reusable source, many possible outputs. A paper, website, and talk still need different editing and emphasis; Quarto reduces duplication rather than making those differences disappear.



Good afternoon, and welcome. I’m Ben Black, and I lead the DML service working group, Data and Modelling Infrastructure for Living Labs, here at ZALF. I prepared this workshop with Isabel Nicholson-Thomas and Manuel Kurmann from ETH Zürich, who are not here today.
The title is deliberately a little dramatic: Quarto does not replace every tool. Think about your last project—your notes, the paper, and perhaps a talk or website. Much of the material overlapped, but you probably rebuilt and reformatted it in several places. Today is about a more modest and useful idea: keeping that material in one coherent source and reusing it across outputs.
Bridge: So what is the problem this is trying to solve?



The individual tools are not necessarily the problem; the friction is at the boundaries between them. We copy text, figures, and references from one place to another, spend time reformatting them, and eventually one version changes while another does not.
Quarto separates the source from the way it is presented. In many cases, producing a webpage rather than a PDF becomes a configuration change instead of a rewrite. That does not mean every output is automatically perfect, and Quarto does not do the research or the editorial thinking for us. It reduces the duplicated packaging work around that research.
Bridge: The workshop moves from that basic idea to concrete examples.



The session has two halves. First, we establish the small set of concepts shared by every Quarto project. Then we apply the same concepts to different research outputs.
The use cases are a menu, not a checklist. You do not need research diaries, manuscripts, presentations, websites, and dashboards all at once; choose what is useful for your own work. The slides give you orientation, but the actual learning starts when you try an exercise in the second half. The workshop website keeps the instructions and examples available afterwards.
Bridge: Let us first build the shared mental model.



These next four slides are essentially all the theory we need today. Keep one sentence in mind: Markdown carries the content, YAML configures the document, and optional code produces results. Quarto renders those ingredients into an output. Everything later is an application of that same model.



Quarto is an open-source publishing system created by Posit, the organisation behind RStudio. “Publishing system” simply means that it takes a source file and turns it into an output such as a document, presentation, or website. It is not a new programming language, and you can use the editor you already know.
If you have used R Markdown, Quarto is the newer and broader continuation of that approach, so much will feel familiar. If you have not, you have not missed a prerequisite: the same overall model works with R, Python, Julia, or with no code at all.
Most .qmd files bring together our three ingredients: Markdown for what we write, YAML for document settings, and optional code chunks for calculations, tables, and figures. We will see code become concrete in the use cases rather than in a separate foundation slide.
Bridge: Putting those ingredients in one source gives us several practical benefits.



First, a .qmd file is plain text. It remains readable without a particular word processor, and version-control tools can show changes line by line. A Word file can of course be revised and tracked, but it is not naturally stored as a human-readable line-by-line document.
Second, the source can be rendered to several formats. This is the source–presentation separation in practice: the target format is largely configuration, although a polished paper and a polished talk will still need some output-specific adjustment.
Third, code can sit beside the explanation it supports. When the document renders, that code can regenerate numbers, tables, and figures from the data. This does not guarantee reproducibility—the data and software environment still matter—but it removes a common source of stale copy-and-paste results.
And for LaTeX users: Quarto’s standard PDF route uses LaTeX underneath, so you keep its typesetting quality while writing most day-to-day structure in lighter syntax.
Bridge: Let us look at the two pieces everyone will use, starting with Markdown.



Markdown is a small set of plain-text conventions for describing structure. For example, ## says “this line is a heading,” and two asterisks say “emphasise this text.” This slide is honestly most of what you need to begin; the less common syntax can be looked up when you need it.
The important mindset is that we describe what something is, not exactly how it should look. We mark a heading rather than choosing its font size and colour. The renderer decides how a heading looks in a webpage, PDF, or slide deck. That separation is what lets the same source adapt to different outputs. The workshop website has the full reference for the exercises.
Bridge: Markdown describes the content. YAML supplies the document-level settings.



YAML is best thought of as a settings panel written as text. In a Quarto file it normally appears at the top, between these two --- lines. Each line is a key: value setting: here, the title and author are metadata, while format: pdf tells Quarto what to produce.
Changing pdf to html changes the target output without rewriting the body. In a real project we may still refine the result for that medium, but the switch itself is this small.
YAML uses indentation to show which options belong together, so spacing is meaningful. If rendering fails before it reaches the document content, this header is one of the first places to check for a misplaced space or colon.
Handover: We now have the complete authoring model: Markdown for content, YAML for configuration, and optional code for results. From here on, we are applying that model to actual research tasks.




Title: Dramatic title, modest promise: overlapping material, one coherent source, reuse across outputs.
Why: The friction is between tools: copying, reformatting, and drifting versions. Reduce duplication, not thought.
Roadmap: Shared foundations first; use cases are a menu; exercises are where learning happens.
Foundations: Markdown = content; YAML = configuration; optional code = results; rendering = output.
What is Quarto?: The publishing step, not a language or editor. Open source, multi-language, three ingredients.

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
Keep returning to this one mental model:

A Quarto source combines Markdown for the content, YAML for the configuration, and, when useful, code for computed results. Quarto renders that source into the output you need.

The deliberately modest version of the promise is one reusable source, many possible outputs. A paper, website, and talk still need different editing and emphasis; Quarto reduces duplication rather than making those differences disappear.

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
Good afternoon, and welcome. I’m Ben Black, and I lead the DML service working group, Data and Modelling Infrastructure for Living Labs, here at ZALF. I prepared this workshop with Isabel Nicholson-Thomas and Manuel Kurmann from ETH Zürich, who are not here today.
The title is deliberately a little dramatic: Quarto does not replace every tool. Think about your last project—your notes, the paper, and perhaps a talk or website. Much of the material overlapped, but you probably rebuilt and reformatted it in several places. Today is about a more modest and useful idea: keeping that material in one coherent source and reusing it across outputs.
Bridge: So what is the problem this is trying to solve?

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
The individual tools are not necessarily the problem; the friction is at the boundaries between them. We copy text, figures, and references from one place to another, spend time reformatting them, and eventually one version changes while another does not.
Quarto separates the source from the way it is presented. In many cases, producing a webpage rather than a PDF becomes a configuration change instead of a rewrite. That does not mean every output is automatically perfect, and Quarto does not do the research or the editorial thinking for us. It reduces the duplicated packaging work around that research.
Bridge: The workshop moves from that basic idea to concrete examples.

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
The session has two halves. First, we establish the small set of concepts shared by every Quarto project. Then we apply the same concepts to different research outputs.
The use cases are a menu, not a checklist. You do not need research diaries, manuscripts, presentations, websites, and dashboards all at once; choose what is useful for your own work. The slides give you orientation, but the actual learning starts when you try an exercise in the second half. The workshop website keeps the instructions and examples available afterwards.
Bridge: Let us first build the shared mental model.

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text: These next four slides are essentially all the theory we need today. Keep one sentence in mind: Markdown carries the content, YAML configures the document, and optional code produces results. Quarto renders those ingredients into an output. Everything later is an application of that same model.

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
Quarto is an open-source publishing system created by Posit, the organisation behind RStudio. “Publishing system” simply means that it takes a source file and turns it into an output such as a document, presentation, or website. It is not a new programming language, and you can use the editor you already know.
If you have used R Markdown, Quarto is the newer and broader continuation of that approach, so much will feel familiar. If you have not, you have not missed a prerequisite: the same overall model works with R, Python, Julia, or with no code at all.
Most .qmd files bring together our three ingredients: Markdown for what we write, YAML for document settings, and optional code chunks for calculations, tables, and figures. We will see code become concrete in the use cases rather than in a separate foundation slide.
Bridge: Putting those ingredients in one source gives us several practical benefits.

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
First, a .qmd file is plain text. It remains readable without a particular word processor, and version-control tools can show changes line by line. A Word file can of course be revised and tracked, but it is not naturally stored as a human-readable line-by-line document.
Second, the source can be rendered to several formats. This is the source–presentation separation in practice: the target format is largely configuration, although a polished paper and a polished talk will still need some output-specific adjustment.
Third, code can sit beside the explanation it supports. When the document renders, that code can regenerate numbers, tables, and figures from the data. This does not guarantee reproducibility—the data and software environment still matter—but it removes a common source of stale copy-and-paste results.
And for LaTeX users: Quarto’s standard PDF route uses LaTeX underneath, so you keep its typesetting quality while writing most day-to-day structure in lighter syntax.
Bridge: Let us look at the two pieces everyone will use, starting with Markdown.

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
Markdown is a small set of plain-text conventions for describing structure. For example, ## says “this line is a heading,” and two asterisks say “emphasise this text.” This slide is honestly most of what you need to begin; the less common syntax can be looked up when you need it.
The important mindset is that we describe what something is, not exactly how it should look. We mark a heading rather than choosing its font size and colour. The renderer decides how a heading looks in a webpage, PDF, or slide deck. That separation is what lets the same source adapt to different outputs. The workshop website has the full reference for the exercises.
Bridge: Markdown describes the content. YAML supplies the document-level settings.

title: Talking points: opening and foundations
text:
YAML is best thought of as a settings panel written as text. In a Quarto file it normally appears at the top, between these two --- lines. Each line is a key: value setting: here, the title and author are metadata, while format: pdf tells Quarto what to produce.
Changing pdf to html changes the target output without rewriting the body. In a real project we may still refine the result for that medium, but the switch itself is this small.
YAML uses indentation to show which options belong together, so spacing is meaningful. If rendering fails before it reaches the document content, this header is one of the first places to check for a misplaced space or colon.
Handover: We now have the complete authoring model: Markdown for content, YAML for configuration, and optional code for results. From here on, we are applying that model to actual research tasks.

A helping hand from AI
text: In case you need yet another reason to make the switch to Quarto: Markdown is (currently) heavily used by AI agents. Because it is a lightweight markup language, chatbots are very proficient at writing in it. It is also the format of the skills (including those written specifically for Quarto) used by agentic AI services like Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex. Both of these services have extensions for VS Code and Positron, so you can use them for assistance directly in your editor.

title: A helping hand from AI
text:
Quarto agent skills
A Skill is a small, self-contained folder of instructions (and sometimes scripts) that an AI agent can load on demand when a task calls for it. Rather than hoping the model remembers the finer points of Quarto syntax from its training data, a Skill hands it up-to-date, task-specific guidance at exactly the moment it is needed. The Posit team maintains an official set of Quarto Skills that you can drop into a Claude- or Codex-enabled IDE and put to work straight away. Three are currently available.

authoring
The workhorse of the collection. It gives the agent comprehensive guidance for writing Quarto documents as Quarto intends: using the hashpipe (#|) cell-option syntax, cross-references, callout blocks, and extensions. It also knows how to migrate existing work: point it at an old R Markdown (.Rmd) file, or a whole bookdown, blogdown, xaringan, or distill project, and it will convert the source to Quarto for you. If you are coming to this workshop from an R Markdown background, this is the Skill to reach for first.


brand-yml
Consistency of style is one of the things brand.yml does best, and this Skill teaches the agent to create and apply one for you. It will discover any existing brand definition in your project and layer your colours, fonts, and logos across every output format (HTML documents, dashboards, RevealJS presentations, Typst PDFs, and full websites), so a single source of truth sets the look of everything you publish. It saves time once you have settled on a personal or institutional identity.


alt-text
Accessible figures are easy to neglect and tedious to write by hand. This Skill generates and improves alt text for both code-generated plots and static images, following Amy Cesal’s three-part formula: the chart type, the data being shown, and the key insight a reader should take away. The result is alt text that tells screen-reader users what the figure shows instead of restating the caption.






Tip



Skills are not magic: they steer the agent towards good practice, but you remain the author. Always read what the agent produces, especially migrations and generated text, before committing it.

title: Writing manuscripts
text:
Everyone knows that managing the drafting, feedback and submission of manuscripts is a lot of work. Some colleagues require .docx format to allow for track changes, some work with LaTeX. Journals each have their own arcane formatting requirements, which are rarely documented correctly in their own author guides.
Using Quarto for manuscripts is not a silver bullet for all these problems, but it does take away a lot of the headaches by keeping narrative text, citations, figures and tables (generated by code or imported) in a single reproducible workflow.

title: Writing manuscripts
section: Key benefits of using Quarto for manuscripts
text:
Key benefits of using Quarto for manuscripts

Multi-format output
One source file renders to several formats, so each need gets the format it wants:

.html or .docx for internal review and sharing with collaborators.
.pdf and .tex (LaTeX) for journal submission. Quarto can also make PDFs with Typst, which is built in and needs no LaTeX installation.

There are quite a number of journal templates available for Quarto that format your manuscript to a specific journal’s requirements. Equally, uploading the .tex file to the journal’s LaTeX submission portal is often the easiest approach.






TipEarly mover advantage



If you are a PhD researcher writing a cumulative thesis and you write each paper with Quarto, combining them into the thesis is much easier. One of the authors of this workshop prepared a template for doing this.




Reproducible figures and tables
When analysis is embedded, manuscript results become easier to update and verify. By setting up a custom ggplot or matplotlib theme in a separate script, you can ensure that all your figures have a consistent style and easily change colours or fonts according to journal requirements without having to manually edit each figure. This also makes it easier to maintain a consistent visual identity across all your publications.






Tip



Long code chunks for figures make a manuscript .qmd hard to read, so it is better to move them into a script. For example, a figures.R script can define a function for each figure. Call source("scripts/figures.R") in a setup chunk at the top of manuscript.qmd, then call one function per figure chunk, so every figure is regenerated from the data each time you render.




Inline statistics from data
Inline code pulls values such as p-values or summary statistics directly from your data, so the text of your manuscript shows the current results without manual updates.
For example, with the restoration data loaded in a setup chunk, you can write the following sentence in your manuscript. Quarto runs the inline code at render time, so if a new monitoring round is added to the data the sentence updates on the next render.

RPython


```{r}
#| include: false
sites <- read.csv("data/restoration-sites.csv")
```

We monitored `r length(unique(sites$site))` restoration sites, with a mean
species richness of `r round(mean(sites$species_richness), 1)` species
per site.


```{python}
#| include: false
import pandas as pd
sites = pd.read_csv("data/restoration-sites.csv")
```

We monitored `{python} sites["site"].nunique()` restoration sites, with a mean
species richness of `{python} round(sites["species_richness"].mean(), 1)`
species per site.



Both versions render as plain text in the finished document, for example: “We monitored 4 restoration sites, with a mean species richness of 14.6 species per site.”


Integrated citation support
You cite a source by typing @ and its key, for example [@gann2019], and Quarto builds the reference list when it renders. The visual editor in RStudio, Positron and VS Code can insert a citation from your Zotero library or directly from a DOI, and it adds the entry to your bibliography (.bib) file for you.
The citation style comes from a CSL file named in the YAML header (csl: journal-style.csl), so you can switch between styles such as APA, Chicago or a journal’s own without reformatting any references by hand.


Cross-referencing
Quarto supports hyperlinked cross-referencing of figures, tables, and sections to keep everything aligned as the manuscript evolves.


Supplementary material management
Supplementary material, including code for reproducing analyses, can be kept in the same project and linked to the main manuscript.

title: Creating websites for research outreach
text:
Quarto allows you to generate full websites which can then be deployed for free using services such as GitHub Pages or Netlify. This provides an easy solution to create web content for research groups, project pages, course and teaching materials, as well as personal academic profiles.

text:
Why researchers build websites
Doing some form of outreach activities has become increasingly important for:

Increasing your professional visibility
Communicating research outputs to audiences beyond academic journals
Sharing research materials and methods with the broader community

title: Creating websites for research outreach
section: The basics of websites with Quarto
text:
The basics of websites with Quarto

Rendering
Quarto websites are built on top of Bootstrap, a free and widely used front-end framework.
Like all websites, Quarto website pages render as HTML files. In RStudio, VS Code and Positron you can view them locally in the viewer pane by clicking the Preview button at the top of the editor window, or by right-clicking the file.


Project-level configuration
Like all Quarto projects, websites should use a project-level _quarto.yml file to define the website structure and formatting. This allows you to easily manage navigation, themes, and other shared settings across all pages of the site.


The front page: index.qmd
Websites must have an index.qmd file in the root directory which serves as the front page of the site. This page can include any content you like, but it is often used to provide an overview of the site and highlight key information.


Reusable authoring patterns
The same Markdown, YAML, callouts, images, and code chunk patterns used in other Quarto output formats can all be used in websites too. You can also include additional HTML or JavaScript blocks or scripts to add custom functionality to your site.






Tip



Websites can include other Quarto content such as dashboards and RevealJS presentations as part of the site, but they are not required to be built with Quarto. You can also include any other content such as PDFs, videos or Google Forms by embedding them with iframes.




Formatting and theming

Built-in themes
Quarto ships with 25 built-in themes drawn from the Bootswatch project (such as cosmo, flatly, journal, and litera). Because a website is a project, you set the theme once in _quarto.yml and every page inherits it:
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
Swap the name to preview alternatives until you find one that fits. The full list is in the Quarto theme documentation.


Customising with Sass and CSS
While a built-in theme gets you most of the way there, it can feel a bit generic. To change things up you can layer your own styling on top. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language browsers read directly to style a page, while Sass is a superset that adds conveniences like variables, nesting, and reusable rules, and it compiles down to plain CSS before the browser sees it. For Quarto, the recommended route is a Sass theme file (.scss), which lets you override Bootstrap variables (colours, fonts, spacing) and add custom rules. You can include this in your project by adding it to the _quarto.yml file:
format:
  html:
    theme:
      - cosmo
      - custom.scss
Inside custom.scss, variables go in a defaults layer and custom rules in a rules layer:
/*-- scss:defaults --*/
$body-bg: #fdfdfd;
$link-color: #2c7fb8;

/*-- scss:rules --*/
.navbar-title { font-weight: 700; }
Alternatively, for small, one-off tweaks a plain CSS file works just as well:
format:
  html:
    css: styles.css






Tip



Sass and CSS run deep, so don’t be afraid to bring in some help. AI chat services and coding agents are good at writing CSS, and there are tools aimed at design work in particular, such as Claude Design, Impeccable and Open Design.




Light and dark mode
Quarto can give a website a light and a dark mode. Provide two themes in the YAML and Quarto adds a toggle to the navbar. The first entry is the default, and each side can be paired with its own .scss:
format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: flatly
      dark: darkly


Building a consistent visual identity
For maintaining a consistent identity across your website, presentations, and reports, Quarto can also read a shared _brand.yml file that defines your colours, fonts, and logo in one place. This is covered in the advanced topics section.

title: Markdown for beginners
text:
Why Markdown is worth learning
Markdown is worth learning because it is:

fast to write
easy to read in raw form
suitable for version control
flexible across websites, reports, and manuscripts

Once you are comfortable with Markdown, you can use most of Quarto.

title: Markdown for beginners
text:
Core syntax

Headings
# Main Title
## Section
### Subsection


Emphasis
*italic* and **bold**


Lists
- bullet item
- another bullet

1. first step
2. second step


Links and images
[Quarto](https://quarto.org)

![Quarto logo](/assets/logo-quarto.svg){width="120px"}


Code
Wrap a short snippet in single backticks to format it as inline code within a sentence.
For longer code, use a fenced block: open with three backticks and a language name, then close with three backticks. The block displays the code with the right syntax highlighting, but does not run it:
```bash
quarto render
```

```python
print("Hello from Python")
```

```r
print("Hello from R")
```
Wrapping the language name in curly braces instead, such as {r}, turns the block into an executable chunk that Quarto runs when the document renders, placing the result in the output.

title: Markdown for beginners
text:
Quarto-focused additions
Quarto keeps standard Markdown, but it also makes room for:

callout blocks for notes, warnings, and tips
cross-references for sections, figures, and tables
executable code chunks
layout features for richer publishing

You do not need to memorise every Markdown feature at once. For most workshop tasks, headings, lists, links, emphasis, and fenced code blocks are enough to get started.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
Quarto is an open-source publishing system developed by Posit. It is built for technical and scientific communication, which makes it especially useful for research settings where writing, analysis, and presentation often belong together.
Quarto is closely related to R Markdown, and many researchers meet it as the newer, broader continuation of ideas that became popular in the R Markdown ecosystem. The biggest shift is that Quarto was designed from the start as a multi-language, multi-format publishing system rather than as a tool mainly associated with R.

title: What is Quarto?
section: Research needs more than one format
text:
Research needs more than one format
Research outputs rarely stay in one format. The same project may need:

notes during exploration
a manuscript draft
conference slides
a project website
an interactive communication piece

Quarto supports all of these with a common syntax and shared project structure. That is the larger theme of this workshop: one authoring system, many academic uses.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
Key strengths

Universal plain-text syntax
Quarto uses readable plain text files with the .qmd extension. A binary format (such as .docx or .xlsx) is stored in a way only its own software can read, so you cannot see what actually changed between two versions of a file. Plain text can: every edit is a visible line that you can track, review, and roll back.






Figure 1: A version-control tool (here GitHub Desktop) showing exactly what changed between two versions of this very page, with added lines in green. This kind of line-by-line history only works because Quarto files are plain text.





Multiple outputs from one source
A single source file can render to many polished outputs: the same content, reshaped for each medium. Here is one short document rendered three different ways:






HTML page







PDF







Word (DOCX)





You write it once; Quarto handles the formatting for each. The same idea extends to slides, dashboards, and full websites, the outputs you will build in the rest of this workshop. In fact, the website you are reading right now was built with Quarto.






NoteIf you know LaTeX



If you have used LaTeX, for example through Overleaf, Quarto will feel familiar: you write in a plain-text source and can produce PDFs with proper mathematical notation. The main difference is that Quarto uses Markdown, which is simpler than LaTeX markup, and renders the same source to other formats as well, such as HTML, Word, and slides, not only PDF. Quarto’s pdf format uses LaTeX internally, so you can still include raw LaTeX where you need it.




Executable code in multiple languages
Quarto can run code inside the document as well as display it. The result below is computed when the page is rendered, not typed in by hand:

2 + 2

[1] 4


Quarto supports R, Python, Julia, and Observable JavaScript. Swap r for python or julia in the chunk header and the same idea works, so everyone can stay in the language they know.






ImportantQuarto, Markdown, and YAML



Most Quarto files combine three ingredients:

YAML for metadata and configuration
Markdown for the written content
optional code chunks for computation and generated output

Two ways to do this exercise
Pick whichever is more useful to you. The steps are the same either way:

Path A: Bring your own. Turn a talk you already need to give (or a recent paper or poster) into a Quarto deck. You will get the most out of the exercise this way, because you end with slides you can actually present.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
The sample data (Path B)
restoration-sites.csv records quarterly monitoring of four restoration sites (A–D) from 2023 to 2025. Each row is one survey of one site:

site: the monitoring site (A–D)
date: survey date (quarterly)
vegetation_cover_pct: vegetation cover, in percent
species_richness: number of species recorded

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Step 1: Create the presentation file
A reveal.js presentation is just one .qmd file with format: revealjs. Make a folder to keep this exercise in (say my-talk/), and inside it create a file called talk.qmd with this minimal starter:
---
title: "Vegetation Recovery Across Four Restoration Sites"
format: revealjs
---

## First slide

Each level-2 heading (`##`) starts a new slide.
Now preview it. Open talk.qmd in your editor and click Preview, or run this in a terminal sitting in the my-talk/ folder:
quarto preview talk.qmd
A slide deck opens in your browser. Use the arrow keys to move through it; press F for fullscreen and Esc to leave. Leave the preview running: it refreshes every time you save.






TipPrefer buttons to typing?



You don’t have to start from scratch. In RStudio choose New File → Quarto Presentation → Reveal JS; in Positron or VS Code open the command palette and pick Quarto: Create Document. The result is the same kind of starter file.








NoteHow slides are made



Two heading levels shape the deck:

# (level 1) creates a section divider: a big title slide that breaks the talk into parts.
## (level 2) creates a content slide.

Everything you write under a ## (text, bullets, a figure) lands on that slide.








NoteA note on the code chunks below



Every R chunk in your real talk.qmd opens with ```{r}, with curly braces, so Quarto runs it. In the sketches on this page we write ```r without braces only so they display as text instead of executing. When you copy them into your file, add the braces back.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
section: Step 2: Add your title slide and author details
text:
Step 2: Add your title slide and author details
The title slide is built automatically from the document’s metadata. Replace the front matter with your own title, a subtitle naming the venue, and a proper author block: add yourself, with an ORCID, email, and affiliation:
---
title: "Vegetation Recovery Across Four Restoration Sites"
subtitle: "iEMSs 2026, Dublin"
author:
  - name: Your Name
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0000
    email: you@institute.org
    affiliations: Your Institute
date: today
format: revealjs
---
Save and watch the preview: the title, subtitle, your name, affiliation, and date now fill the opening slide. This is the same author schema you used in the manuscript exercise, which is what lets you switch themes later without touching it.






NoteWhere to find an ORCID



Every researcher can register for a free ORCID at orcid.org. It is the 16-digit ID in their profile URL. Use a real one if you have it; the placeholder above still renders fine.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Step 3: Add a logo
A conference talk usually carries a logo: your institution’s, or the conference’s. Download the iEMSs 2026 logo (or use your own university’s):
Download iemss2026_logo.png
Save it next to talk.qmd. Then tell reveal.js to use it. To add options to a format, you expand the single-line format: revealjs into a nested block:
format:
  revealjs:
    logo: iemss2026_logo.png
    footer: "Vegetation recovery, iEMSs 2026"
logo: pins your image to the bottom-right of every slide; footer: adds a line of text along the bottom. Render and you will see both.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Step 4: Build your introductory slides
A talk needs a way in. Add a section divider and an opening content slide before you reach any results. Two reveal.js features make these feel like slides rather than a wall of text:

a list wrapped in a ::: {.incremental} block reveals its bullets one click at a time;
a line containing just . . . (three full stops separated by spaces) inserts a pause, and the content after it appears on the next click.

# Background {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Why monitor restoration?

::: {.incremental}
- Restoration projects *promise* recovery, but do sites actually recover?
- We surveyed four sites every quarter for two years
- That gives a simple, testable signal: change in vegetation cover
:::

## Our question

. . .

How fast is vegetation cover recovering, and does the pace differ by site?
The # Background line is a section slide (the {background-color=...} gives it a coloured backdrop), and the two ## lines are content slides. Click through the preview to see the bullets and the pause reveal in turn.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
section: Step 5: Load your data in a setup chunk
text:
Step 5: Load your data in a setup chunk
Your results slide will draw a figure from the data, so load it once near the top. Make a data/ folder inside my-talk/ and copy restoration-sites.csv into it (use the download button above). Then add a setup chunk just below the front matter. include: false runs the code but keeps it, and any messages, off your slides:
```r
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

sites <- read_csv("data/restoration-sites.csv") |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

first  <- sites |> filter(date == min(date))   # earliest survey per site
latest <- sites |> filter(date == max(date))   # most recent survey per site
```
first and latest give the start and end of the monitoring period, which the next slide uses.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
section: Step 6: Add a content slide with a figure and a main message
text:
Step 6: Add a content slide with a figure and a main message
This is the central slide of the talk. A good results slide makes one point, so put the message in the slide title and let a figure carry the evidence. Use a two-column layout to set the chart beside a few takeaways:
## Cover is recovering at every site {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
```r
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(sites, aes(date, vegetation_cover_pct, colour = site)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vegetation cover (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
- Cover rose at **all four** sites
- Site D leads; Site C lags
- Mean cover is up **`r round(mean(latest$vegetation_cover_pct) - mean(first$vegetation_cover_pct))` points** since 2023
:::

::::
Three things to notice:

echo: false shows the plot but hides the code that made it, which is what an audience wants.
The :::: {.columns} / ::: {.column} blocks split the slide; adjust the width percentages to taste.
That last bullet uses inline R, `r ...`, so the headline number is computed from the data, exactly as in the manuscript exercise. Change the CSV and the slide updates itself.

The {.smaller} after the title shrinks the text on this one slide, which helps when a slide is busy.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Step 7: Add speaker notes
Reveal.js has a presenter view that shows notes only you can see. Add a ::: {.notes} block to the bottom of your results slide:
## Cover is recovering at every site

<!-- your columns / figure / bullets from Step 6 -->

::: {.notes}
Remind the audience these are synthetic data. Point out Site C's slow start,
likely the driest site. Pause here for questions before moving on.
:::
The notes never appear on the slide itself. To read them while presenting, press S in the browser to open speaker view: a separate window with your notes, a timer, and a preview of the next slide.






TipHandy presenter keys



With the deck open in a browser: S opens speaker view, F goes fullscreen, O shows a slide overview grid, and E switches to a print layout for exporting to PDF.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
section: Step 8: Switch between the built-in themes
text:
Step 8: Switch between the built-in themes
Quarto ships with a set of reveal.js themes. Pick one with a theme: line under the format:
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: serif
    logo: iemss2026_logo.png
    footer: "Vegetation recovery, iEMSs 2026"
Now try a few: swap serif for simple, moon, solarized, sky, league, night, or dracula and watch the preview restyle instantly. The content stays the same and only the look changes.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Step 9: Try the community “clean” theme
For a more distinctive title slide, install a community theme: Grant McDermott’s widely used quarto-revealjs-clean. From a terminal inside your my-talk/ folder:
quarto add grantmcdermott/quarto-revealjs-clean
This adds an _extensions/ folder providing a new format, clean-revealjs. Switch to it by changing only the format line: the clean theme understands the same reveal.js options, so your logo and footer carry over:
format:
  clean-revealjs:
    logo: iemss2026_logo.png
    footer: "Vegetation recovery, iEMSs 2026"
Render again. Your title slide now uses the clean theme’s layout, and because the author block from Step 2 follows Quarto’s standard schema, your name, ORCID, and affiliation slot straight into it. Changing one line and leaving everything else untouched is possible because content and styling are kept separate.






NoteWhere custom formats come from



clean-revealjs is a Quarto extension: a small bundle of CSS and templates that adds a new output format. It is the same mechanism behind the journal templates in the manuscript exercise. Browse more at the Quarto extensions listing.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Step 10: Render to HTML
While writing you have been using quarto preview. For the finished file, render it:
quarto render talk.qmd
This produces talk.html and a folder talk_files/ that holds the styles, scripts and figures the deck needs. Open talk.html in any modern browser to present; no internet connection or server is required. To share the deck, send both the file and the folder.






TipMake it one shareable file



To bundle everything into a single HTML file you can email or put on a USB stick, add one line under the format:
format:
  revealjs:
    embed-resources: true
Use the format name you ended up with (revealjs or clean-revealjs). The chalkboard in the stretch tasks does not work together with embed-resources, so remove this line again before you try it.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Stretch tasks
If you finish early, try one of these:

Compare management scenarios. Read restoration-scenarios.csv in your setup chunk and add a results slide with a second figure coloured or faceted by scenario (Baseline, Moderate, Intensive). This is the same data behind the scenarios dashboard.
Embed an interactive chart. Reuse a plotly chart from the dashboard exercise on a slide. It stays live and hoverable in the browser, which PowerPoint cannot do.
Animate a transition. Put {auto-animate=true} on two consecutive ## slides and move or resize an element between them; reveal.js tweens it. Or set transition: slide under the format for a global slide transition.
Add a chalkboard. Set chalkboard: true under the format, then press C while presenting to draw on the current slide, or B to open a blank chalkboard. This needs embed-resources to be off.
Export a PDF or PowerPoint. Press E and then print to PDF from the browser (Ctrl + P) for a handout, or add pptx: default to the format: block and render again for a PowerPoint version colleagues can edit.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Adapting Path A (your own talk)
Converting a talk of your own follows exactly the same skeleton:

Put your real title-slide details in the front matter, and your institution’s logo next to the file.
Break your talk into # section dividers and ## content slides, one message per slide.
Re-create your key figure as a code chunk with echo: false (or drop in an image with ![](figure.png)).
Move the script you would otherwise read aloud into ::: {.notes} blocks.
Try a built-in theme, then clean-revealjs, and keep whichever fits your message.

title: Exercise: build a reveal.js presentation
text:
Self-check

Does quarto render talk.qmd produce a talk.html you can open in a browser?
Does the title slide show your name, affiliation, and the logo?
Does at least one slide carry a figure drawn from the data, under a single clear message?
Do your speaker notes show up in speaker view (press S) but never on the slides themselves?
Can you switch from a built-in theme to clean-revealjs by changing only the format: line?

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Build a real Quarto manuscript project: a single source that renders to both a web article (HTML) and a PDF, with full author metadata, a figure drawn from data, summary numbers pulled straight from that data, and a citation. A final optional step applies a journal template. Along the way you will see how project: type: manuscript turns one folder into a small scholarly publishing pipeline.
This is the hands-on companion to the Writing manuscripts page. The full reference for everything below is the Quarto manuscript authoring guide.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Build a real Quarto manuscript project: a single source that renders to both a web article (HTML) and a PDF, with full author metadata, a figure drawn from data, summary numbers pulled straight from that data, and a citation. A final optional step applies a journal template. Along the way you will see how project: type: manuscript turns one folder into a small scholarly publishing pipeline.
This is the hands-on companion to the Writing manuscripts page. The full reference for everything below is the Quarto manuscript authoring guide.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
section: Two ways to do this exercise
text:
Two ways to do this exercise
Pick whichever is more useful to you. The steps are the same either way:

Path A: Bring your own. Take a current or previous research project or manuscript of your own and rebuild its skeleton as a Quarto manuscript. You will get the most out of the exercise this way, because you end with something you can actually keep working on.
Path B: Use our sample data. Build a mock manuscript about ecological restoration from the two datasets below. Choose this if you would rather not wrangle your own data right now.

Wherever a step needs concrete code, we show it for the sample data. If you are on Path A, swap in your own file names, columns, and text.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
The sample data (Path B)
restoration-sites.csv records quarterly monitoring of four restoration sites. Each row is one survey of one site:

site: the monitoring site (A–D)
date: survey date (quarterly)
vegetation_cover_pct: vegetation cover, in percent
species_richness: number of species recorded
soil_moisture_pct: soil moisture, in percent

Download restoration-sites.csv Download restoration-scenarios.csv
(restoration-scenarios.csv holds vegetation cover under three management scenarios and is only needed for the stretch task.)

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Step 1: Create the manuscript project
A manuscript is a project, not a single file, so let Quarto scaffold the folder for you. In your terminal, move to wherever you keep projects and run:
quarto create project manuscript my-manuscript
Quarto asks for a title (press Enter to accept the folder name) and then makes a folder my-manuscript/ with the three files a manuscript needs:

index.qmd is the article itself: metadata, narrative text, and code, all in one file.
_quarto.yml holds the project settings. The line project: type: manuscript tells Quarto to treat this folder as a manuscript and build the article website.
references.bib is your bibliography. Citations you add in the visual editor land here automatically.







TipPrefer buttons to typing?



You don’t have to use the terminal. In RStudio choose New Project → Quarto Manuscript; in Positron or VS Code open the command palette and pick Quarto: Create Project → Manuscript Project. The result is the same starter folder.


Open the folder in your editor and switch index.qmd to the visual editor (the Source / Visual toggle in RStudio or Positron). It makes adding authors, figures, and citations much easier in the steps below.






NoteA note on the code chunks below



Every R chunk in your real index.qmd opens with ```{r}, with curly braces, so Quarto runs it. In the sketches on this page we write ```r without braces only so they display as text instead of executing. When you copy them into your file, add the braces back.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Step 2: Add your authors
Open index.qmd. Replace the starter front matter (everything between the two --- lines) with your own title and a proper author block. You can delete the placeholder section below it. Add yourself and one co-author (pick a real colleague), each with an ORCID, email, and affiliation. This is the scholarly metadata Quarto uses to build the byline in every output format. number-sections: true numbers your headings, which Step 7 needs to refer to a section.
---
title: "Vegetation Recovery Across Four Restoration Sites"
author:
  - name: Your Name
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0000
    corresponding: true
    email: you@institute.org
    affiliations:
      - name: Your Institute
        department: Department of Ecology
        city: Your City
        country: Your Country
  - name: A Colleague
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0001
    corresponding: false
    affiliations:
      - name: Their Institute
        department: Department of Soil Science
date: today
number-sections: true
bibliography: references.bib
---






NoteWhere to find an ORCID



Every researcher can register for a free ORCID at orcid.org. It is the 16-digit ID in their profile URL. Use real ones if you have them; the placeholders above will still render fine.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Step 3: Choose your output formats
The output formats of a manuscript are listed in _quarto.yml. Open it and replace everything in it with:
project:
  type: manuscript

format:
  typst: default
  html: default
typst makes a PDF with Typst, a typesetting system that is built into Quarto, so there is nothing extra to install. html is the article webpage.
Two details matter here:

Keep the PDF format first in the list. On Quarto 1.8, the version that comes with RStudio, the PDF fails with a “file not found” error for figures if html is listed before it. Newer versions accept either order.
The starter _quarto.yml contains execute: freeze: true. With that setting Quarto reuses saved results instead of running your code again, so a change to the data would not show up in the article. Replacing the file as above removes it, which is what you want while you are still writing.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
section: Step 4: Load your data in a setup chunk
text:
Step 4: Load your data in a setup chunk
Make a data/ folder inside my-manuscript/ and copy restoration-sites.csv into it (use the download button above). Then add a setup chunk near the top of index.qmd, below the front matter. include: false runs the code but keeps it and its output out of the article:
```r
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

sites <- read_csv("data/restoration-sites.csv") |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

latest <- sites |> filter(date == max(date))   # most recent survey per site
first  <- sites |> filter(date == min(date))   # earliest survey per site
```
latest and first give us the start and end of the monitoring period, which the next two steps use.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
section: Step 5: Pull summary numbers into your text with inline code
text:
Step 5: Pull summary numbers into your text with inline code
This is the main gain of a reproducible manuscript: numbers in the prose come from the data, so they cannot drift out of sync with it. Inline R code uses single backticks, `r expr`. Start a Methods section with a heading, then write an opening paragraph like this:
## Methods {#sec-methods}

We monitored vegetation recovery at `r n_distinct(sites$site)` restoration
sites across `r n_distinct(sites$date)` quarterly surveys. Mean vegetation
cover rose from `r round(mean(first$vegetation_cover_pct))`% at the first
survey to `r round(mean(latest$vegetation_cover_pct))`% at the most recent,
an increase of `r round(mean(latest$vegetation_cover_pct) - mean(first$vegetation_cover_pct))`
percentage points.
When rendered, the backticked expressions become real values (4 sites, 8 surveys, and so on). Change the CSV and the sentence updates itself.
## makes a level 2 heading, and {#sec-methods} gives it a label so that you can refer to the section in Step 7. Because the front matter sets number-sections: true, it renders as “1 Methods”. In RStudio, the Outline button at the top right of the editor lists your headings; click one to jump to it.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
section: Step 6: Add a figure from code
text:
Step 6: Add a figure from code
Add a code chunk that draws a ggplot figure. The fig- prefix on the label makes it cross-referenceable, and fig-cap gives it a numbered caption:
```r
#| label: fig-cover
#| fig-cap: "Vegetation cover at four restoration sites, quarterly 2023–2025."

ggplot(sites, aes(date, vegetation_cover_pct, colour = site)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vegetation cover (%)", colour = "Site") +
  theme_minimal()
```
Then refer to it in your text. Quarto turns @fig-cover into “Figure 1” and links to it:
Cover increased at every site over the monitoring period (@fig-cover).

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
section: Step 7: Refer to a section and add a citation
text:
Step 7: Refer to a section and add a citation
In the visual editor, start a new paragraph at the end and type “The survey design in”. Choose Insert → Cross Reference and pick sec-methods. Quarto inserts @sec-methods, which renders as “Section 1” and links to the heading, just as @fig-cover did for the figure. In Source mode, type @sec-methods directly.
Continue the sentence, put your cursor where the citation should go and choose Insert → Citation. The dialog can pull references straight from a DOI or from your Zotero library (as well as Crossref, PubMed, and DataCite):

From a DOI: paste a DOI and Quarto fetches the full reference. For example, try 10.1111/rec.13035 (the SER international standards for ecological restoration).
From Zotero: if you have Zotero installed and the integration enabled, search your own library by author or title.

Either way, Quarto inserts an @citation-key in your text, appends the entry to references.bib, and adds a formatted reference list at the end on render. A sentence like:
The survey design in @sec-methods follows recognised restoration standards [@gann2019].
renders the section reference and the citation in text and the full reference under a References heading. The key Quarto creates may differ slightly from gann2019; use whichever key appears in your text.






TipNo visual editor, or the DOI lookup does not respond?





Add the reference by hand. Paste this entry at the end of references.bib, then cite it in your text with [@gann2019]:
@article{gann2019,
  title   = {International principles and standards for the practice of ecological restoration. Second edition},
  author  = {Gann, George D. and McDonald, Tein and Walder, Bethanie and Aronson, James and Nelson, Cara R. and Jonson, Justin and Hallett, James G. and Eisenberg, Cristina and Guariguata, Manuel R. and Liu, Junguo and Hua, Fangyuan and Echeverría, Cristian and Gonzales, Emily and Shaw, Nancy and Decleer, Kris and Dixon, Kingsley W.},
  journal = {Restoration Ecology},
  volume  = {27},
  number  = {S1},
  year    = {2019},
  doi     = {10.1111/rec.13035}
}









TipSwitching citation styles



references.bib stores the facts; a CSL style decides the formatting. To format references for a specific journal, add a csl: line to your front matter pointing at a style file (browse thousands at the Zotero Style Repository). No re-typing required.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
section: Step 8: Render to PDF and HTML
text:
Step 8: Render to PDF and HTML
Build all formats at once by running this in a terminal inside the my-manuscript/ folder:
quarto render
The results land in a new _manuscript/ folder. Open _manuscript/index.html in your browser: the article shows your byline, the inline numbers, the figure, and the references. In the margin, an Other Formats section offers a download link to the PDF, which is _manuscript/index.pdf.
While writing, the Render button in your editor gives a quick preview. In a manuscript project, RStudio’s Render button shows only the HTML article; the PDF is built only by quarto render or by Render Project in the Build tab. quarto preview in a terminal shows the first format in your list instead, here the PDF, and refreshes it on every save.






WarningSection references need numbered sections



If the PDF fails with “cannot reference heading without numbering”, check that the front matter contains number-sections: true. Typst, which makes the PDF, can only refer to numbered headings. The HTML preview does not show this error.








NoteWhat just happened



quarto render ran your R code, placed the results in the text and the figure, and laid the same content out twice: as a web page and as a typeset PDF. Rendering several formats from one source is the main reason to write a manuscript in Quarto.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Step 9: Apply a journal template (optional)
Journals expect their own layout. Quarto maintains a set of journal templates at github.com/quarto-journals, including Elsevier, PLOS, ACS (American Chemical Society), AGU (American Geophysical Union), ACM, and JSS (Journal of Statistical Software).
These templates use LaTeX, so this step needs a LaTeX installation. If you do not have one, Quarto can install TinyTeX, a small LaTeX distribution, for you. The download and the first PDF render, which fetches missing LaTeX packages, can each take several minutes, so start this step only if you have the time and a good connection:
quarto install tinytex
Then add a template from inside the my-manuscript/ folder. We use Elsevier as a general-purpose example:
quarto add quarto-journals/elsevier
This installs an extension into a new _extensions/ folder. The extension provides a new format, elsevier-pdf. Swap it in for typst in _quarto.yml, keeping it first in the list:
project:
  type: manuscript

format:
  elsevier-pdf: default
  html: default
Run quarto render again. The PDF now follows the Elsevier article layout, and nothing in index.qmd had to change. Each journal extension names its formats after the journal, so use plos-pdf, acs-pdf or agu-pdf if you install a different one.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Stretch tasks
If you finish early, try one of these:

Add an abstract and keywords to the front matter (abstract: | and keywords:) and see them appear in both outputs.
Add a table from the data, for example the latest reading per site with knitr::kable(). Give it a #| label: tbl- and cross-reference it with @tbl-....
Compare scenarios. Read restoration-scenarios.csv and add a second figure faceted or coloured by scenario (Baseline, Moderate, Intensive).
Add a Word output for collaborators who want track changes: add docx: default at the end of the format: block and render again.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Adapting Path A (your own manuscript)
Converting your own work follows exactly the same skeleton:

Paste your existing prose into index.qmd under Introduction / Methods / Results / Discussion headings.
Drop your data into data/ and your analysis into the setup chunk (or source() a separate script; see the tip on the Writing manuscripts page).
Replace every hard-typed statistic in your Results with inline `r ...` code.
Re-create your key figure as a labelled code chunk and cross-reference it.
Import your existing .bib (or pull citations from Zotero) and cite with @key.

title: Exercise: write a reproducible manuscript
text:
Self-check

Does quarto render produce both an HTML article and a PDF in _manuscript/ without errors?
Does the byline show you and your co-author, with ORCIDs and affiliations?
Do the numbers in your opening paragraph come from inline code, not typed by hand?
Does @fig-cover render as a numbered, clickable “Figure 1”?
Does @sec-methods render as “Section 1” and link to the Methods heading?
Does your citation appear in the text and in a References list, with the entry now in references.bib?

title: Exercise: build a dashboard
text:
Build a small, interactive Quarto dashboard from monitoring data: a row of headline numbers, a chart, and a table, all drawn from the same source. Along the way you will see how format: dashboard arranges a page into rows and columns.
This is what you are building toward:


The complete, ready-to-run version lives in the repository as dashboards/restoration-dashboard.qmd, so you can copy exact code from there or compare as you go.






NoteYours will look slightly different



The version above inherits this website’s custom fonts and colours. A fresh dashboard uses Quarto’s default styling, so expect the same layout with a plainer look.




You will use a small synthetic dataset, data/restoration-sites.csv. Each row is one survey of one site:


# A tibble: 6 × 5
  site   date       vegetation_cover_pct species_richness soil_moisture_pct
  <chr>  <date>                    <dbl>            <dbl>             <dbl>
1 Site A 2023-04-01                   51               13                28
2 Site A 2023-07-01                   57               13                23
3 Site A 2023-10-01                   55               14                26
4 Site A 2024-01-01                   53               15                34
5 Site A 2024-04-01                   60               15                28
6 Site A 2024-07-01                   66               16                23


It has five columns:

site: the monitoring site (A to D)
date: survey date (quarterly)
vegetation_cover_pct: vegetation cover, in percent
species_richness: number of species recorded
soil_moisture_pct: soil moisture, in percent

Download restoration-sites.csv



A dashboard is an ordinary .qmd file with one decisive setting: the output format in the YAML header is set to dashboard.
---
title: "My Dashboard"
format: dashboard
---
Everything else, the Markdown, the code chunks, stays exactly as you know it. What changes is how Quarto arranges the content on the page, which is what the next section is about.



This part trips most people up at first, so it is worth getting clear before you build.
A dashboard fills the browser window and arranges your content into a grid of cards. Two heading levels control that grid:

## starts a new row
### starts a new column inside the current row

By default a dashboard is row-oriented: rows stack from top to bottom, and cards placed in the same row sit side by side.
One row, two columns (charts side by side):
## Row

### Column
```r
chart_one
```

### Column

You will use a small synthetic dataset, data/restoration-sites.csv. Each row is one survey of one site:


# A tibble: 6 × 5

title: Exercise: build a dashboard
text:
Build it step by step
Create a file my-dashboard.qmd in your project folder, and place the downloaded CSV in a subfolder called data next to it. The snippets below assume exactly this layout, so the path data/restoration-sites.csv is relative to your .qmd file; adjust it if you store the CSV somewhere else. And remember: add the curly braces around r in every code cell you copy.

Step 1: Header and setup
---
title: "Restoration Site Monitoring"
format: dashboard
execute:
  echo: false
---

```r
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)
library(DT)

sites <- read_csv("data/restoration-sites.csv") |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

latest <- sites |>
  filter(date == max(date))

first <- sites |>
  filter(date == min(date))
```
echo: false hides the code, so the dashboard shows only results, and include: false keeps this setup cell from becoming a card of its own. The chunk loads the packages and the data, then prepares two subsets: latest keeps the most recent survey per site (used by the value boxes and the table), and first keeps the earliest one, so we can show how much cover has changed.


Step 2: Add a row of headline numbers
A value box is a code cell with #| content: valuebox that returns a small list:
## Row

```r
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Sites monitored"
list(value = n_distinct(sites$site), icon = "geo-alt", color = "primary")
```

```r
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Surveys recorded"
list(value = nrow(sites), icon = "clipboard-data", color = "secondary")
```

```r
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Cover change since 2023"
list(value = paste0("+", round(mean(latest$vegetation_cover_pct) - mean(first$vegetation_cover_pct)), " pts"),
     icon = "graph-up-arrow", color = "success")
```
The value can be any small computation: n_distinct(sites$site) counts the unique sites, nrow(sites) counts the rows (one per survey), and the third box subtracts the mean cover of the first survey round from the mean of the latest one to get the change in percentage points.
Render. Three coloured boxes appear side by side, three cards in one row. The icon names come from the Bootstrap Icons library, where you can browse all available icons and copy their names.






TipYou can put plain text on a dashboard too



A card does not have to hold code. Write a short paragraph in its own row to add a description, exactly as the finished dashboard does at the top:
## Row {height="15%"}

Vegetation cover is recovering across all four restoration sites.




Step 3: Chart vegetation cover over time
## Row

```r
#| title: "Vegetation cover over time"
plot_ly(sites, x = ~date, y = ~vegetation_cover_pct, color = ~site,
        type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = ""), yaxis = list(title = "Cover (%)"),
         legend = list(title = list(text = "")))
```
plot_ly() builds the chart from the sites data: x and y say which columns go on the axes, color = ~site draws one line per site, and type/mode make it a line chart with visible points (the ~ tells plotly to look the name up as a column). The layout() call afterwards just tidies up the axis titles and the legend.
Render and hover the lines to read values. That is plotly’s interactivity, and it needs no server.


Step 4: Put a table of the latest readings beside the chart
A dashboard card can hold a table just as easily as a chart. Give the row two explicit columns, the chart in one and a sortable DT table in the other:
## Row

### Column
```r
#| title: "Vegetation cover over time"
plot_ly(sites, x = ~date, y = ~vegetation_cover_pct, color = ~site,
        type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = ""), yaxis = list(title = "Cover (%)"),
         legend = list(title = list(text = "")))
```

### Column
```r
#| title: "Latest readings by site"
latest |>
  select(Site = site,
         `Cover (%)` = vegetation_cover_pct,
         `Richness` = species_richness,
         `Soil moisture (%)` = soil_moisture_pct) |>
  datatable(options = list(dom = "t"), rownames = FALSE)
```
The table cell works in two steps: select() picks the columns to show and renames them into readable headers (backticks allow spaces like `Cover (%)`), then datatable() turns the result into an interactive table. The option dom = "t" shows only the table itself, without a search box or pagination, and rownames = FALSE drops the row numbers.
Render. The chart and the table now sit side by side under the value boxes. Click a column header in the table to sort it. That is your finished dashboard.

title: Exercise: build a dashboard
text:
Stretch: a what-if scenario explorer (optional)
To give the dashboard the feel of an interactive tool, you can let readers switch between precomputed views with a tabset. We provide a second dataset, data/restoration-scenarios.csv, holding vegetation cover under three management scenarios (Baseline, Moderate, Intensive).
Download restoration-scenarios.csv
Here is what it produces. Switch the tabs above the chart to compare the scenarios:


Read it in your setup chunk and add a small helper function. The helper wraps the whole chart recipe once, so each tab later needs only a single line; filter() keeps just the rows of the chosen scenario:
scenarios <- read_csv("data/restoration-scenarios.csv") |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

plot_cover <- function(scenario_name) {
  scenarios |>
    filter(scenario == scenario_name) |>
    plot_ly(x = ~date, y = ~vegetation_cover_pct, color = ~site,
            type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers") |>
    layout(xaxis = list(title = ""),
           yaxis = list(title = "Cover (%)", range = c(30, 95)),
           legend = list(title = list(text = "")))
}
Then turn one column into a tabset, with one tab per scenario:
### Column {.tabset}

```r
#| title: "Baseline (no action)"
plot_cover("Baseline")
```

```r
#| title: "Moderate restoration"
plot_cover("Moderate")
```

```r
#| title: "Intensive restoration"
plot_cover("Intensive")
```
Because all three charts share a fixed y-axis (range = c(30, 95)), switching tabs shows the real difference rather than plotly rescaling each one. It feels like a what-if explorer, yet every view is precomputed, so the page is still fully static.

Create a Quarto document for documenting ongoing research activity in a structured, readable way.

title: Exercise: build a research diary

Prerequisites
You should be familiar with:

title: Exercise: build a research diary
text:
Starter scenario
Choose one recent decision, comparison, or exploratory step from your own modelling work. This does not need to be a major result.
Examples include:

Choosing between two environmental datasets
Excluding, transforming, or aggregating observations

title: Exercise: build a research diary

Step-by-step exercise
